title: IV. The Second Ordeal
paragraphs: “You have no idea how much you encourage us, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, by your willingness to answer,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, with an animated air and obvious satisfaction beaming in his very prominent, short-sighted, light gray eyes, from which he had removed his spectacles a moment before. “And you made a very sound point about mutual trust — without it, in cases of this importance, it is sometimes simply impossible to make headway, if the suspect genuinely hopes and wishes to defend himself and is in a position to do so. For our part, we will do everything in our power, and you can see for yourself how we are conducting the case. Do you approve, Ippolit Kirillovitch?” He turned to the prosecutor.
“Oh, certainly,” replied the prosecutor. His tone was somewhat cool compared with Nikolay Parfenovitch’s impulsiveness.

I will note once and for all that Nikolay Parfenovitch, who had only recently arrived in our town, had from the very first developed a marked respect for Ippolit Kirillovitch, our prosecutor, and had become almost his bosom friend. He was nearly the only person who placed complete faith in Ippolit Kirillovitch’s extraordinary gifts as a psychologist and orator, and in the justice of his grievance. He had heard of him in Petersburg. On the other hand, young Nikolay Parfenovitch was the only person in the whole world whom our “underappreciated” prosecutor genuinely liked. On their way to Mokroe they had found time to reach an understanding about the present case. And now, as they sat at the table, the sharp-witted junior caught and interpreted every indication on his senior colleague’s face — half a word, a glance, or a wink.
“Gentlemen, just let me tell my own story and don’t interrupt me with trivial questions, and I’ll tell you everything in a moment,” said Mitya excitedly.

“Excellent! Thank you. But before we proceed to hear what you have to say, will you allow me to inquire about another small fact of great interest to us? I mean the ten roubles you borrowed yesterday at around five o’clock, against the security of your pistols, from your friend Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin.”
“I pawned them, gentlemen. I pawned them for ten roubles. What else? That is all there is to it. As soon as I got back to town, I pawned them.”
“You got back to town? Then you had been out of town?”
“Yes, I went forty versts into the country. Didn’t you know?”
The prosecutor and Nikolay Parfenovitch exchanged glances.

“Well, how would it be if you began your account with a systematic description of everything you did yesterday, starting from the morning? Allow us, for example, to inquire why you were absent from town, and exactly when you left and when you came back — all those facts.”

“You should have asked me like that from the start,” cried Mitya, laughing out loud. “And if you like, we won’t begin from yesterday, but from the morning of the day before; then you’ll understand how and why and where I went. The day before yesterday, gentlemen, I went to a merchant of the town called Samsonov, to borrow three thousand roubles from him on reliable security. It was an urgent matter, gentlemen, a sudden necessity.”
“Allow me to interrupt you,” the prosecutor put in politely. “Why were you in such urgent need of exactly that sum — three thousand?”

“Oh, gentlemen, you needn’t go into details — how, when, why, why just that much money and not some other amount, and all that rigmarole. It will run to three volumes, and then you’ll want an epilogue!”
Mitya said all this with the good-natured but impatient familiarity of a man who is determined to tell the whole truth and is full of the best intentions.

“Gentlemen!” — he corrected himself hurriedly — “don’t be annoyed with me for being restless, I beg you again. Believe me once more, I have the greatest respect for you and understand the true state of affairs. Don’t think I’m drunk. I’m quite sober now. And besides, even being drunk would be no obstacle. It’s with me, you know, like the saying: ‘When he’s sober, he’s a fool; when he’s drunk, he’s a wise man.’ Ha ha! But I see, gentlemen, it isn’t appropriate to crack jokes with you until we’ve had our explanation out. And I have my own dignity to preserve, too. I quite understand the difference between us at this moment. After all, I am in the position of a criminal, and so far from being on equal footing with you. And it’s your job to keep watch on me. I can’t expect you to pat me on the head for what I did to Grigory — you can’t go breaking old men’s skulls and get away with it. I suppose you’ll lock me up for him for six months, maybe a year, in a house of correction. I don’t know what the punishment is — but it will be without loss of the rights of my rank, without loss of my rank, won’t it? So you see, gentlemen, I understand the distinction between us.... But you must admit that you could baffle God Himself with such questions. ‘How did you step? Where did you step? When did you step? And on what did you step?’ I’ll get myself tangled up if you go on like this, and you’ll write it all down against me. And what will that lead to? To nothing! And even if I’m talking nonsense now, let me finish, and you, gentlemen, being men of honor and refinement, will forgive me! I’ll finish by asking you, gentlemen, to abandon that conventional method of questioning. I mean, beginning with some miserable trifle — how I got up, what I had for breakfast, how I spat, and where I spat — and so distracting the criminal’s attention, and then suddenly stunning him with an overwhelming question: ‘Whom did you murder? Whom did you rob?’ Ha ha! That is your standard method, that’s where all your cunning comes in. You can catch peasants off guard that way, but not me. I know the tricks. I was in the service, too. Ha ha ha! You’re not angry, gentlemen? You’ll forgive my impertinence?” he cried, looking at them with a good nature that was almost astonishing. “It’s only Mitya Karamazov, you know, so you can let it pass. It would be inexcusable in a sensible man, but in Mitya it’s forgivable. Ha ha!”

Nikolay Parfenovitch listened, and laughed as well. Although the prosecutor did not laugh, he kept his eyes fixed sharply on Mitya, as if anxious not to miss the slightest syllable, the slightest movement, the smallest twitch of any feature of his face.

“That is how we have treated you from the beginning,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, still laughing. “We haven’t tried to throw you off by asking how you got up in the morning and what you had for breakfast. We actually began with questions of the greatest importance.”

“I understand. I saw it and appreciated it, and I appreciate still more your present kindness to me — an unprecedented kindness, worthy of your noble hearts. The three of us here are gentlemen, and let everything be on a footing of mutual confidence between educated, well-bred people, who share the common bond of noble birth and honor. In any case, allow me to regard you as my best friends at this moment of my life, at this moment when my honor is under attack. That’s no offense to you, gentlemen, is it?”
“On the contrary. You’ve expressed all that so well, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Nikolay Parfenovitch answered with dignified approval.
“And enough of those petty questions, gentlemen — all those tricky questions!” Mitya cried enthusiastically. “Otherwise there’s simply no knowing where we’ll end up! Isn’t that so?”

“I will follow your sensible advice entirely,” the prosecutor interposed, addressing Mitya. “I don’t withdraw my question, however. It is now vitally important for us to know exactly why you needed that sum, precisely three thousand.”
“Why I needed it?... Oh, for one thing and another.... Well, it was to pay a debt.”
“A debt to whom?”

“That I absolutely refuse to answer, gentlemen. Not because I couldn’t, or because I wouldn’t dare, or because it would be damaging — for it is all a petty matter and completely trivial — but because it is a matter of principle: this is my private life, and I will not allow any intrusion into my private life. That’s my principle. Your question has no bearing on the case, and whatever has nothing to do with the case is my private affair. I wanted to pay a debt. I wanted to pay a debt of honor, but to whom, I will not say.”
“Allow me to make a note of that,” said the prosecutor.
“By all means. Write down that I won’t say, that I won’t. Write that I should consider it dishonorable to say. Ech! you can write it; you’ve nothing else to do with your time.”

“Allow me to caution you, sir, and to remind you once more, in case you are unaware of it,” the prosecutor began, with a peculiar and stern emphasis, “that you have every right not to answer the questions put to you now, and we, for our part, have no right to force an answer from you, if you decline to give one for one reason or another. That is entirely a matter for your personal decision. But it is our duty, on the other hand, in cases such as this, to explain and make clear to you the degree of injury you will be doing yourself by refusing to give this or that piece of evidence. With that, I beg you to continue.”
“Gentlemen, I’m not angry ... I ...” Mitya muttered in a rather disconcerted tone. “Well, gentlemen, you see, that Samsonov I went to then ...”

We will, of course, not repeat his account of what the reader already knows. Mitya was impatiently anxious not to omit the slightest detail. At the same time, he was in a hurry to get it over with. But as he gave his evidence, it was being written down, and so they had continually to stop him. Mitya disliked this, but submitted; he grew angry, though still good-humoredly. It’s true he did exclaim from time to time, “Gentlemen, that’s enough to make an angel lose his patience!” Or, “Gentlemen, it’s no good your irritating me.”

But even as he exclaimed, he still kept for a time his genially expansive mood. He told them how Samsonov had made a fool of him two days earlier. (By now he had fully realized that he had been fooled.) The sale of his watch for six roubles to get money for the journey was something new to the lawyers. They were at once keenly interested, and even, to Mitya’s intense indignation, thought it necessary to write down the fact as secondary confirmation that he had barely a kopeck in his pocket at the time. Little by little, Mitya began to grow sullen. Then, after describing his trip to see Lyagavy, the night spent in the stifling hut, and so on, he came to his return to town. Here he began, without particular prompting, to give a detailed account of the agonies of jealousy he suffered on Grushenka’s account.

He was heard in silent attention. They inquired especially into the fact that he had a place of ambush in Marya Kondratyevna’s house at the back of Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden, to keep watch on Grushenka, and that Smerdyakov had brought him information. They placed particular emphasis on this and wrote it down. Of his jealousy he spoke warmly and at length, and though inwardly ashamed at exposing his most intimate feelings to “public indignity,” so to speak, he evidently overcame his shame in order to tell the truth. The cold severity with which the investigating lawyer, and still more the prosecutor, stared intently at him as he told his story, in the end thoroughly disconcerted him.

“That boy Nikolay Parfenovitch, to whom I was talking nonsense about women only a few days ago, and that sickly prosecutor, are not worth my telling this to,” he reflected mournfully. “It’s humiliating. ‘Be patient, humble, hold thy peace.’” He wound up his reflections with that line. But he pulled himself together and went on. When he came to telling of his visit to Madame Hohlakov, he regained his spirits and even wanted to tell a little anecdote about that lady, one that had nothing to do with the case. But the investigating lawyer stopped him, and civilly suggested that he move on to “more essential matters.” At last, when he described his despair and told them how, on leaving Madame Hohlakov’s, he had thought that he would “get three thousand even if he had to murder somebody to do it,” they stopped him again and wrote down that he had “meant to murder someone.” Mitya let them write it without protest. At last he reached the point in his story when he learned that Grushenka had deceived him and had returned from Samsonov’s as soon as he had left her there, although she had said she would stay until midnight.

“If I didn’t kill Fenya then, gentlemen, it was only because I had no time,” he suddenly blurted out at that point in his story. That, too, was carefully written down. Mitya waited gloomily, and was beginning to tell how he had run into his father’s garden, when the investigating lawyer suddenly stopped him, and opening the big portfolio that lay on the sofa beside him, he brought out the brass pestle.
“Do you recognize this object?” he asked, showing it to Mitya.
“Oh, yes,” he laughed gloomily. “Of course I recognize it. Let me have a look at it.... Damn it, never mind!”
“You forgot to mention it,” observed the investigating lawyer.
“Hang it all, I wouldn’t have concealed it from you. Do you suppose I could have managed without it? It simply slipped my memory.”
“Be so good as to tell us precisely how you came to arm yourself with it.”
“Certainly I will be so good, gentlemen.”
And Mitya described how he had taken the pestle and run.
“But what purpose did you have in mind, arming yourself with such a weapon?”
“What purpose? No purpose. I just picked it up and ran off.”
“What for, if you had no purpose?”

Mitya’s anger flared up. He looked intently at “the boy” and smiled gloomily and spitefully. He was feeling more and more ashamed at having told “such people” the story of his jealousy so sincerely and spontaneously.
“To hell with the pestle!” he suddenly burst out.
“But still —”
“Oh, to fend off dogs.... Oh, because it was dark.... In case something came up.”
“But have you ever before taken a weapon with you when you went out, since you’re so afraid of the dark?”

“Ugh! damn it all, gentlemen! There’s simply no talking to you!” cried Mitya, exasperated beyond endurance, and turning to the secretary, crimson with anger, he said quickly, with a note of fury in his voice:

“Write down at once ... at once ... ‘that I snatched up the pestle to go and kill my father ... Fyodor Pavlovitch ... by hitting him on the head with it!’ Well, now are you satisfied, gentlemen? Are your minds at rest?” he said, glaring defiantly at the lawyers.

“We quite understand that you made that statement just now out of exasperation with us and the questions we put to you, which you consider trivial, though they are in fact essential,” the prosecutor remarked dryly in reply.

“Well, for heaven’s sake, gentlemen! Yes, I took the pestle.... What does one pick things up for at such moments? I don’t know what for. I snatched it up and ran — that’s all. For my part, gentlemen, passons, or I swear I won’t tell you another thing.”

He sat with his elbows on the table and his head in his hand. He sat sideways to them and stared at the wall, struggling against a wave of nausea. He had, in fact, a terrible urge to get up and declare that he would not say another word, “not if you hang me for it.”

“You see, gentlemen,” he said at last, with difficulty getting hold of himself, “you see. I listen to you and am haunted by a dream.... It’s a dream I have sometimes, you know.... I often dream it — it’s always the same ... that somebody is hunting me, somebody I’m dreadfully afraid of ... that he’s hunting me in the dark, in the night ... tracking me, and I hide somewhere from him, behind a door or a cupboard, hide in some degrading way, and the worst of it is, he always knows where I am, but pretends not to know where I am on purpose, to prolong my agony, to enjoy my terror.... That is just what you’re doing now. It’s exactly like that!”
“Is that the sort of thing you dream about?” inquired the prosecutor.
“Yes, it is. Don’t you want to write it down?” said Mitya, with a twisted smile.
“No; no need to write it down. But still you do have curious dreams.”
“It’s not a question of dreams now, gentlemen — this is realism, this is real life! I’m a wolf and you’re the hunters. Well, hunt him down!”
“You are wrong to make such comparisons ...” began Nikolay Parfenovitch, with extraordinary gentleness.

“No, I’m not wrong, not at all!” Mitya flared up again, though his outburst of anger had obviously eased his heart. He grew more good-humored with every word. “You may not trust a criminal, or a man on trial being tortured by your questions, but an honorable man, the honorable impulses of the heart (I say that boldly!) — no! That you must believe, you have no right not to ... but —
Be silent, heart, Be patient, humble, hold thy peace.
Well, shall I go on?” he broke off gloomily.
“If you would be so kind,” answered Nikolay Parfenovitch.
